title: NHIS Health Inequality Trends
summary: A reproducible SAS pipeline estimating 25-year trends in income-related inequality in self-rated health, using pooled NHIS data from 1997 to 2024.
overview: This study examines long-term trends in income-related inequality in self-rated health among non-elderly U.S. adults, by gender and race/ethnicity, using the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). By harmonizing 27 survey waves spanning 1997 to 2024, the work supports population-level inequality estimates that are comparable across major survey redesigns. The results feed a manuscript in preparation (Cubbin & Zhong) on 25-year trends in health inequality.
myRole: I build and maintain the harmonization and analytic workflow for the study, focusing on methodological consistency, cross-period comparability, and correct handling of complex survey design. I work in coordination with the faculty investigator on analytic specifications and manuscript preparation.

sections.title: Data Harmonization & Survey Processing
content: Harmonized 27 years of NHIS data (1997 to 2024) across major redesigns (1997 and 2019), resolving changes in variable definitions, coding schemes, weights, and sample design.
Standardized income-to-poverty ratio (PIR) categories, demographic definitions, and exclusion criteria to keep estimates comparable across pooled periods.
Documented the 2019 redesign's effects, including increased race/ethnicity missingness and PIR invariance, as explicit analytic decisions.

sections.title: Inequality Measures & Analytic Methods
content: Computed the Slope Index of Inequality (SII), Relative Index of Inequality (RII), and ridit-based rankings using design-adjusted survey procedures.
Applied design-based variance estimation with sampling weights, strata, and PSUs, and combined 10 multiple-imputation implicates under Rubin's rules.
Produced design-adjusted SII and RII estimates across multiple demographic domains and pooled periods, with trend tests and trend figures.

sections.title: Quality Assurance & Reproducibility
content: Established reproducible protocols including drift checks, cross-tab validation, and missingness diagnostics that catch data issues before analysis.
Maintained version-controlled outputs, a harmonization rulebook, and analytic decision records to support transparent, replicable survey research.
Collaborated with the faculty investigator to refine analytic specifications and prepare results for publication.

technologies: Complex survey methods (weights, strata, PSUs, variance estimation)
outcomes: Harmonized 27 NHIS survey waves (1997 to 2024) into an analysis-ready, version-controlled dataset.
Generated design-adjusted SII, RII, and ridit-based inequality estimates with trend tests across pooled periods.
Improved analytic reliability and reproducibility through standardized QA protocols and documented analytic decisions.
Supported a manuscript in preparation on 25-year trends in income-related inequality in self-rated health (Cubbin & Zhong).
